props.title: Dinosaur

sections.content: Dinosaur (2000) marked a fascinating turning point in Disney's animation evolution, blending groundbreaking CGI characters with live-action backgrounds. Following the success of Jurassic Park (1993), dinosaur films experienced a renaissance, but Disney took a radically different approach. Instead of going for terror, they crafted a migration epic featuring Aladar, an Iguanodon raised by lemurs. The film's $127 million budget was astronomical for 2000, with much spent on capturing real-world locations that would be populated by digital characters - a technique that wouldn't become common until The Jungle Book (2016).

sections.content: The technical achievements of Dinosaur overshadowed its story innovations. It was one of the first major animated films to tackle themes of Darwinian survival and natural selection in a way accessible to children. While The Land Before Time (1988) touched on loss, Dinosaur directly addressed extinction-level events and adaptation. The film's opening sequence - a dialogue-free tour de force following a dinosaur egg's journey - remains one of Disney's most experimental pieces of storytelling. SUBHEAD: The CGI Revolution

Dinosaur sits at a crucial moment in animation history, between the hand-drawn era and the CGI dominance that would follow with films like Ice Age (2002) and Pixar's The Good Dinosaur (2015). Its production methods influenced later hybrid films like The Lion King (2019), which also used photorealistic characters against natural backgrounds. The film's attention to paleontological accuracy - while still maintaining artistic license for character design - set a new standard for depicting prehistoric life in family entertainment.
